title: THE TRAVEL RULE CAME TO CRYPTO
subtitle: THE BLOCKCHAIN WAS ONLY ONE DATA LAYER.

blocks.text: A TRANSACTION CAN REVEAL LITTLE ON-CHAIN WHILE AN INSTITUTION COLLECTS IDENTITY DATA BESIDE IT.
CRYPTO HAS MORE THAN ONE RECORD.

When people debate blockchain privacy, they often stare only at the chain. Regulated exchanges and other virtual asset service providers operate another layer: customer records, deposit and withdrawal histories, risk systems and information exchanged for compliance.

The Financial Action Task Force's standards require covered virtual asset service providers to apply preventive measures including customer due diligence, record keeping and suspicious transaction reporting. Its Travel Rule framework also calls for originator and beneficiary information to be obtained, held and securely transmitted for covered transfers.
01 // THE TRAVEL RULE IS NOT A BLOCKCHAIN FEATURE

The Travel Rule does not require Bitcoin, Zcash or another base protocol to write a passport name into a block. It is a regulatory obligation applied to covered service providers. The identity-information channel and the blockchain transaction can therefore exist as separate but related records.

That distinction is important. Protocol privacy can reduce what the public ledger reveals while a regulated intermediary may still know its customer and retain information required by applicable law. Privacy from the public and privacy from a service provider are different threat models.
SHIELDED DOES NOT MEAN KYC NEVER HAPPENED. KYC DOES NOT MEAN THE ENTIRE WORLD NEEDS THE TRANSACTION GRAPH.
02 // IMPLEMENTATION IS EXPANDING

FATF's July 2026 targeted update reported that 83 percent of surveyed jurisdictions had passed legislation implementing the Travel Rule, up from 73 percent in 2025. FATF also said significant implementation and supervision gaps remain. The direction is clear even if the global regime is not uniform.

Rules differ by jurisdiction, transaction type and service-provider status. A global standard-setting body's recommendation is also not itself the domestic law of every country. Specific obligations depend on how jurisdictions implement those standards.
03 // SELF-CUSTODY CHANGES THE PATH

A peer-to-peer transfer between self-custodied wallets is architecturally different from a transfer processed by two custodial exchanges. There may be no VASP in the middle maintaining the same customer-account relationship. Regulators nevertheless continue to focus on risks involving peer-to-peer activity and unhosted wallets, especially where regulated services interact with them.

FATF's 2026 work specifically discusses stablecoins, peer-to-peer transfers and unhosted wallets. That does not mean every self-custodied transaction is prohibited or automatically subject to identical information-sharing requirements. It means the boundary between regulated services and user-controlled wallets is an active compliance focus.
04 // TWO GRAPHS CAN EXIST

One graph is technical: addresses, transactions, commitments, nullifiers or other protocol data. Another is institutional: accounts, identity records, timestamps, deposit addresses, withdrawal requests and compliance messages. On a transparent chain, those layers can sometimes reinforce each other. With shielded transfers, the public transaction graph can reveal substantially less even though an exchange still retains its own records.

This is why saying 'the blockchain is private' or 'the exchange knows who you are' does not settle the privacy question. Both can be true in different scopes. The relevant question is which observer receives which information.
PRIVACY IS NOT ONE SWITCH. IT IS A MAP OF WHO GETS TO KNOW WHAT.
05 // THE ARGUMENT CRYPTO KEEPS MISSING

Compliance and public surveillance are not synonyms. A regulated institution can be required to know its customer without requiring every unrelated observer on the internet to receive that customer's payment history. Conversely, a public blockchain can expose transaction relationships even when no institution knows the identity behind an address.

Those are separate architectural choices. Collapsing them into a single debate about whether privacy is compatible with regulation hides the more useful question: what information must be available to which party, under what authority, and why should anyone else receive it?
